content.title: About
content.content: Atlantic haddock (Melanogrammus aeglefinus) is a marine fish of the cod family that lives in the cold waters of the North Atlantic. Its fillet is light‑gray, has a delicate flavor and a slightly sweet aroma. Haddock is widely used in cooking for baking, frying, poaching and making fish cakes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Haddock is one of the most popular fish in the United Kingdom, often served as part of "fish and chips".
Compared with cod, haddock has finer scales and a more tender flesh.
Haddock can grow up to 80 cm in length and weigh more than 5 kg.
In the wild, haddock migrates in search of food, often following larger predators such as whales.
Haddock is used to produce fish mince and canned fish products.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: Haddock fillet provides about 20 g of high‑quality protein per 100 g, supporting tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: It is a lean fish, making it suitable for calorie‑controlled diets.

items.title: Contains omega‑3 fatty acids
items.content: Haddock supplies EPA and DHA, which are beneficial for heart and brain health.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: The fish is a good source of vitamin B12, niacin and riboflavin, important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Haddock provides selenium, iodine and phosphorus, essential for thyroid function and bone health.

items.title: Fish allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to seafood, including haddock.

items.title: Mercury content
items.content: While haddock generally has low mercury levels, pregnant women and young children should limit intake.

items.title: Nutrient loss with high heat
items.content: Over‑cooking can reduce omega‑3 levels and heat‑sensitive vitamins.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Haddock can be baked with herbs, fried in a light batter, poached in broth, or steamed. The fillet pairs well with lemon, dill and olive oil. For extra tenderness, you can briefly soak the fish in milk before cooking.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep fresh haddock in the refrigerator at 0‑2 °C, wrapped in plastic film or in an airtight container, and use within 2 days. For longer storage, freeze it in a sealed bag at –18 °C, where it remains good for up to 3 months. Before cooking, check the smell: the fish should smell fresh, without a strong ammonia odor.
